Case built for teaching: the starting CT is real (public archive) and without trauma; laceration, hematoma, clot and free blood were added by computer with the noise of the original image. The small mass of the left kidney, by contrast, is real.
In blunt trauma the spleen is the most frequently injured solid organ. On the 2018 AAST scale: grade I subcapsular hematoma < 10% of the surface or laceration < 1 cm; grade II hematoma 10-50%, intraparenchymal < 5 cm or laceration 1-3 cm; grade III hematoma > 50% or expanding, intraparenchymal ≥ 5 cm or laceration > 3 cm; grade IV vascular injury with bleeding contained within the spleen, or laceration of segmental or hilar vessels with devascularization > 25%; grade V shattered spleen or active bleeding extending into the peritoneum. Here the laceration is about 3.5-4 cm deep, in any case more than 3 cm: grade III.
The sentinel clot (denser than free blood, 45-70 HU) lies near the bleeding organ: it helps find the source when the blood has already spread. Free blood should be sought in the dependent sites (perihepatic and Morison pouch, paracolic gutters, rectovesical or Douglas pouch) and is denser than urine.
Pitfalls: in the early arterial phase the normal spleen can be heterogeneous with a "zebra" pattern and mimic lacerations (here the phase is later and the healthy parenchyma is homogeneous); left shoulder pain (Kehr sign) is due to diaphragmatic irritation. Treatment depends mainly on hemodynamic status: in the stable patient non-operative management is often chosen, with embolization if vascular injuries appear.
Incidental finding: even in an emergency the small renal mass is described and its characterization is recommended once the patient is stable.
